1	# emotely
2	
3	A daily journaling app with an AI **Journaling Assistant** that walks you through
4	a structured reflection — up to 10 topics per session — and produces a summarized
5	journal entry. This is a ground-up rebuild of the original emotely (a shipped
6	Flutter + Firebase app, sunset in early 2025) around a modern, tools-first AI
7	harness.
8	
9	Three goals, held at once:
10	
11	1. **Personal use** — I journal with it daily.
12	2. **Public AI-engineering showcase** — the agent service and the Flutter GenUI
13	   client are both open (MIT) and meant to be read.
14	3. **Fund spare-time work** — a 5€/month subscription with high margins.
15	
16	## Decisions
17	
18	The load-bearing decisions and their rationale live in [`docs/adr/`](docs/adr/):
19	
20	1. [Monorepo](docs/adr/0001-monorepo.md) — agent + app + shared contract in one repo
21	2. [Tools-first harness](docs/adr/0002-tools-first-harness.md) — tool calls, not prompted JSON
22	3. [Model gateway + cost ceiling](docs/adr/0003-model-gateway-and-cost-ceiling.md) — provider-agnostic, cheap-model constraint
23	4. [PostHog observability stack](docs/adr/0004-posthog-observability-stack.md) — full bundle, no Sentry
24	5. [Journal content privacy](docs/adr/0005-journal-content-privacy-mode.md) — `privacyMode` on, metadata only
25	6. [Flutter iOS + Android only](docs/adr/0006-flutter-ios-android-only.md) — no web, demand-driven expansion
26	7. [Protected `main`](docs/adr/0007-protected-main-for-autonomous-agents.md) — PR + CI gate, because agents write here
27	
28	The project's language is defined in [`CONTEXT.md`](CONTEXT.md).
29	
30	## Architecture
31	
32	Monorepo. Two apps that share one contract, plus Supabase (data/auth) and
33	PostHog (analytics + the self-driving loop).
34	
35	```
36	emotely/
37	├─ apps/
38	│  ├─ agent/      TypeScript · Vercel AI SDK agent loop · deploys to Vercel
39	│  │             tools: ask_topic / record_answer / complete_session
40	│  │             evals/ — offline fixtures → cost + quality (CI gate)
41	│  └─ app/        Flutter (iOS + Android) · renders one native widget per tool call
42	├─ packages/
43	│  └─ contract/   the tool-call schema — single source of truth for both sides
44	└─ README.md
45	```
46	
47	### Why a monorepo
48	
49	The agent and the app are two halves of one product joined by **one contract**:
50	the agent emits tool calls, the app renders a native widget per call. That shared
51	schema (`packages/contract`) must never drift between producer and consumer — in a
52	monorepo a schema change plus both sides move in one atomic, CI-verified commit.
53	Solo founder → one CI, one release story, one front door. Both repos are public
54	anyway, so the usual "keep one half private" argument doesn't apply.
55	
56	Tooling stays boring: pnpm workspaces for the TS side, Flutter's own tooling for
57	`apps/app`, path-filtered GitHub Actions. No Nx/Turbo/Bazel.
58	
59	### The stack
60	
61	| Layer | Choice | Why |
62	|---|---|---|
63	| **Client** | Flutter, iOS + Android only (no web) | Native GenUI story; VGV/Flutter-community audience |
64	| **Agent runtime** | TypeScript · Vercel AI SDK · Vercel | Tools-first agent loop, streaming, the AI-eng showcase |
65	| **Model access** | Gateway (Vercel AI Gateway **or** OpenRouter) | Swap models via config; benchmark cheap models on real sessions |
66	| **Data + auth** | Supabase (Postgres + Auth) | Fresh schema, no Firebase baggage |
67	| **Observability** | PostHog (full bundle, see below) | LLM obs, flags, experiments, error tracking, Max AI |
68	| **Subscriptions** | RevenueCat | Known quantity from the original app |
69	| **License** | MIT, both apps | Portfolio-friendly, maximally reusable |
70	
71	### Tool-calling replaces the old JSON hack
72	
73	The original assistant ran on the Firebase GenAI Chatbot extension: a ~2KB prompt
74	that *begged* the model to emit parseable JSON (`response` + `summary`), with a
75	"recovery prompt" retry when the JSON didn't parse. That's fighting the model.
76	
77	The rebuild gives the model **tools** instead:
78	
79	- `ask_topic(topic, input_type)` — `input_type ∈ text | color_picker | mood_slider | multi_select`; the client renders the matching native widget. **This is the generative UI.**
80	- `record_answer(topic, value)` — structured, validated tool args. No JSON-parsing prayer.
81	- `complete_session(summary)` — the summary is a validated tool argument, not parsed prose.
82	
83	The old `ColorText` / `ColorTextEditingController` feature becomes just one
84	`input_type` (`color_picker`).
85	
86	## PostHog — the "self-driving" layer
87	
88	Adopted day one (all free at our scale, ~0€ at 1k MAU):
89	
90	- **Product analytics** — `posthog_flutter` (app) + `posthog-node` (agent).
91	- **LLM observability** — `@posthog/ai` with `experimental_telemetry` on AI SDK
92	  calls → `$ai_generation` events (tokens, cost, latency, traces per model).
93	  **`privacyMode` ON** — journal text never leaves the device to PostHog; only
94	  metadata is captured. Non-negotiable for a journaling app.
95	- **Feature flags + experiments** — a flag payload `{ model, prompt }` drives
96	  **server-side model selection** in the agent, no deploy. PostHog's **LLM prompt
97	  experiments** auto-attribute cost + quality per variant.
98	- **Error tracking** — native PostHog exception tracking. **No Sentry.**
99	- **Max AI + anomaly alerts** — agentic analyst that watches AI-cost-per-user and
100	  session-completion and pings on drift. This is the self-driving watchdog.
101	- **Session replay + surveys** — deferred (replay only with mask-all-text, given
102	  sensitive journal content).
103	
104	**The self-driving loop:** PostHog flag hands the agent `{model, prompt}` →
105	`@posthog/ai` emits cost/latency per variant → LLM prompt experiment attributes
106	cost + quality per variant → Max AI / anomaly alerts flag drift. The product tunes
107	its own model choice; you get pinged instead of dashboard-staring.
108	
109	Set **billing limits / spike protection** per product on day one — a retry storm
110	must not surprise-bill.
111	
112	## Cost model (the hard constraint)
113	
114	A daily poweruser (~30 sessions/month, ~10 topics each) must cost **well under
115	50¢/month**, ideally a few cents, inside a 5€ sub with high margins.
116	
117	- Frontier models (Claude Sonnet/Opus) — **out**, blow the budget per session.
118	- Haiku-class — borderline (~$1.50–2.70/mo).
119	- **Gemini Flash-Lite / GLM-4.x-class** — a few cents to ~60¢/mo, and the only
120	  tier that hits "a few cents."
121	- **Prompt caching** on the static context prompt cuts session cost 3–5× — this
122	  matters more than the exact model.
123	- The task is narrow and well-specified (10 fixed topics, extract → summarize) —
124	  a cheap model with good tool-calling is enough. No frontier reasoning needed.
125	
126	Final model is chosen **empirically** at build time via the eval harness + a
127	PostHog LLM prompt experiment, not from memory.
128	
129	## Two layers of evaluation
130	
131	1. **Offline evals** (`apps/agent/evals/`) — deterministic fixtures replayed
132	   against each candidate model. The CI gate; catches regressions before ship.
133	   Seed from the original app's `promptfoo` conversation fixtures.
134	2. **Online experiment** (PostHog) — real sessions, real cost, live variant
135	   comparison. The self-driving loop.
136	
137	Offline proves *correct + cheap in the lab*; online proves *cheap + retained in
138	the wild*.
139	
140	## Build order
141	
142	1. **`apps/agent` skeleton** — Vercel AI SDK loop, the three tools, gateway wired,
143	   one cheap model hardcoded. Prove a full 10-topic session runs end-to-end via
144	   tool calls. No client yet.
145	2. **Offline eval harness** — port the original prompt + `promptfoo` conversation
146	   fixtures into `evals/`. CI gate: replay, assert correctness, measure cost per
147	   candidate.
148	3. **Benchmark** — run evals across GLM-4.x / Gemini Flash-Lite / Haiku; pick the
149	   cheapest that passes. Add prompt caching. Confirm poweruser cost. **Decide the
150	   gateway here** (OpenRouter has a dedicated PostHog install path; Vercel AI
151	   Gateway is "supported" — pick by integration cleanliness).
152	4. **PostHog online** — `@posthog/ai` (privacyMode on), flag-driven model
153	   selection, first LLM prompt experiment.
154	5. **`apps/app`** — Flutter shell rendering a widget per tool call, Supabase auth +
155	   entry persistence, `posthog_flutter`.
156	6. **Subscription + polish** — RevenueCat, paywall, ship to TestFlight.
157	
158	## Verify-at-build-time (do NOT pin from memory)
159	
160	Per project convention, research the latest before pinning:
161	
162	- Vercel AI SDK, `@posthog/ai`, `posthog-node`, `posthog_flutter` versions.
163	- Current GLM and Gemini Flash-Lite model IDs (note: "GLM 5.2" does not exist —
164	  current is the GLM-4.x line; confirm exact version).
165	- Gateway choice (OpenRouter vs Vercel AI Gateway) — settle at step 3 empirically.
166	
167	## Legacy
168	
169	The original app lives at `~/dev/emotely-legacy` (Flutter + Firebase, sunset early
170	2025). Worth cherry-picking, not migrating: the context/opening/recovery prompt
171	design, the `promptfoo` conversation fixtures, the `ColorText` idea, and the strong
172	accessibility bar (a11y tests for every view). Everything else — the Firebase
173	GenAI extension, the JSON-recovery hack, Firestore, Sentry, the web target — is
174	gone.

Research agent is running in the background against the installed CLI and the official docs; it'll write the doc to the repo.

On your second question — **where to keep tooling context so agents know it exists:**

[CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) is the discovery point — it's the one file every agent session loads automatically, so anything not reachable from there effectively doesn't exist for an agent. But it should stay short, so the pattern that fits this repo's existing convention (README → `docs/adr/`, `CONTEXT.md`):

- **`docs/tooling/<tool>.md`** — one short doc per tool: what it does, key commands, agent-relevant caveats. That's where the Entire doc is being written (`docs/tooling/entire.md`).

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled — the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Each question should be formatted like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree — settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent to find it — don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report — ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's — put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

41	- **the agent** (`apps/agent`) — the deployed TypeScript service running the
42	  tool-calling loop.
43	- **an autonomous agent** — an AI coding agent that writes to this repository.
44	  These are the actors [ADR 0007](docs/adr/0007-protected-main-for-autonomous-agents.md)
45	  protects `main` against.

47	## Gate
48	
49	A check that must pass *before* a change lands. Distinct from a **rollback**,
50	which is a correction *after*. The CI gate is a precondition; rollback is the
51	second line of defence. See [ADR 0007](docs/adr/0007-protected-main-for-autonomous-agents.md).

55	Two distinct layers, never used interchangeably:
56

58	  against candidate models. A CI gate. Proves *correct and cheap in the lab*.
59	- **Online experiment** (PostHog) — real sessions, live variant comparison.

content.text:
I've got everything I need for round 1 — including a find: the legacy context prompt survives in `~/dev/emotely-legacy/backend/extensions/firestore-genai-chatbot.env`, and it reveals that in the original app **topics were given to the assistant** (with per-topic format instructions and answer counts), not invented by the model. That shapes several questions below.

Here's the frontier — 9 independent decisions. Answers to these unblock the next round (contract details, state shape, model ID research).

---

❓ **Q1** - **Where do topics come from?**: The README says "up to 10 topics per session", ADR 0003 says "10 fixed topics". The legacy prompt was *handed* a topic set per date ("You will be given a set of topics... Each topic comes with instructions"). For the rebuild: (a) a fixed hardcoded topic list the agent walks through, (b) a configurable list passed into the session (per-user/per-date later), or (c) the model chooses topics freely? And is `ask_topic`'s `topic` argument then an enum from that list or a free string?

➡️ (b) with (a)'s content for now: the session loop takes a topic list as input, skeleton hardcodes one default list of 10. `topic` stays a free string in the contract (the list is session config, not schema) — enum would force a contract change per topic tweak.

❓ **Q2** - **How does the user's answer flow back?**: Two viable loop shapes. **(a) Client-executed tool:** `ask_topic` is a tool the *client* answers — its tool result carries the raw widget value back to the model, which then calls `record_answer` with the normalized, validated value. **(b) Plain chat turn:** the widget answer comes back as a user message; the model calls `record_answer` from it. (a) is the AI SDK generative-UI idiom and keeps the transcript structured end-to-end; (b) is simpler but re-introduces prose-parsing at the seam.

➡️ (a). `ask_topic` = client-side tool (no `execute` on the agent; the driver/Flutter app supplies the result), `record_answer` = server-side tool that validates and stores. This makes the CLI driver an honest stand-in for the Flutter client.

❓ **Q3** - **How is `record_answer.value` typed?**: (a) A discriminated union per input type — `text` → string, `mood_slider` → number in a fixed range, `color_picker` → hex string, `multi_select` → string array. (b) Just a string, interpret later.

➡️ (a). The contract is the single source of truth the Flutter side renders against; a stringly-typed `value` would smuggle the old JSON-parsing problem back in through the side door.

❓ **Q4** - **One answer per topic, or several?**: The legacy prompt had "number of answers required" per topic and examples show it collecting *multiple* answers ("What else did you learn?"). CONTEXT.md currently implies one ask/one record per topic. Does v1 allow multiple `record_answer` calls per topic?

➡️ Allow multiple: the contract doesn't forbid it (same `topic` on repeated calls just appends), and the topic list input carries an optional per-topic hint like the legacy design. Costs nothing in schema, matches how the assistant actually behaved.

❓ **Q5** - **Runtime shape for #2**: Local-only session loop invoked by the CLI driver, or also an HTTP endpoint deployed to Vercel now?

➡️ Local only. The loop is a plain async function (`runSession(config, io)`); the CLI driver is one consumer, the Vercel route becomes a second consumer when the Flutter client lands (#6). No deploy in #2.

❓ **Q6** - **What is the CLI driver?**: (a) Interactive — you journal in the terminal via stdin, real dogfooding from day one. (b) Scripted — canned answers, deterministic run.

➡️ (a) interactive. Deterministic replay is exactly what issue #3 (offline evals) builds — building a scripted driver now would duplicate it a week early. And "I journal with it daily" starts working at #2 instead of #6.

❓ **Q7** - **Which gateway to wire first?**: ADR 0003 defers the *final* vendor to issue #4, but the skeleton needs one wired now: Vercel AI Gateway or OpenRouter?

➡️ Vercel AI Gateway. Native to the AI SDK (model is a `'provider/model'` string — the "swappable via config" criterion becomes a single env var), one key, you deploy to Vercel anyway. OpenRouter gets its fair fight in #4 as the ADR intends.

❓ **Q8** - **System prompt source**: Adapt the legacy CONTEXT prompt (found it — it encodes real learned behavior: one topic at a time, the off-topic-redirect discipline, tone/emoji, treat off-topic remarks as data for the current topic) or write a minimal fresh one?

➡️ Adapt legacy. Strip everything that existed to serve the JSON hack and the "topics given as text" mechanism (tools replace both); keep the behavioral core. It's also the prompt the #3 eval fixtures were written against, so continuity helps there.

❓ **Q9** - **Session end + guardrails**: A session ends when the model calls `complete_session`. What about: the user saying "I'm done" mid-session (model should skip remaining topics and complete), and a runaway loop (model never completes)? Also: is the test story for #2 TDD with the AI SDK's mock language model, with the live 10-topic run as the manual acceptance check — or do you want live-model assertions in CI already?

➡️ User can end early → prompt instructs model to call `complete_session` with what it has. Hard cap via the SDK's step limit (~3 steps per topic + slack) as the runaway guard. TDD with mock model in CI; live run stays manual until #3 makes it an eval.

---

Answer in any form ("all as recommended, except Q4: …" works). Round 2 will cover what these unblock: exact contract v1 fields, session-state shape, prompt-caching posture in the skeleton, and the concrete cheap-model ID (that one's a research task I'll dispatch, not a question).

Q1: Ask a subagent to gather additional context on how this was handled. The user was able to choose from pre-existing question/topic sets before starting a session. The chosen set was ingested into the context at the start of the session. So (b). `topic` should be a somewhat free string, because in the end the user should be able to create their own question sets.

Q2: (a)

Q3: Research in the existing app. We had multi-answer, long text, color, emoji and rating. Let's stick with this initially and adjust later.

Q4: Long text is single answer, multi-answer (usually like "what are you grateful for today?") has multiple answers, emoji and color we could allow multiple answers if we want and rating is a single answer.

Q5: agreed

Q6: agreed

Q7: agreed

Q8: agreed

Q9: agreed, although I'd say we need more data for the step limit. For example if someone wants to record 10 or even 20 things they're grateful for, we want to allow that. So a generous limit is what we will aim for now. We can then adjust and think about UX patterns that make restricting it more transparent to the user
Good — Q2, Q5–Q8 settled, Q9 with a generous step limit. Q1 and Q3 both need legacy research; dispatching one subagent for both now.

# Legacy emotely: question sets & input types

## 1. The set concept: `JournalQuestionSet`

Not "topic set" or "template" — the code says **question set**. The word "topic" appears *only* in the LLM context prompt in `firestore-genai-chatbot.env`; there is zero occurrence of "topic" in the Dart codebase. The app calls them questions.

Three-layer model, and the split matters:

**`JournalQuestion`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_question.dart`
```dart
required String id;                          // Firestore doc id
required Translations localizations;         // Map<String,String>, lang code -> question text
required JournalQuestionAnswerType type;     // the input type
@Default(<String>[]) List<String> tags;       // DEAD — never read anywhere
int? minAnswers;                              // null => treated as 1
int? maxAnswers;                              // DEAD — never enforced anywhere
```
`Translations = Map<String, String>` (`/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/typedefs.dart:10`). Localization falls back to `localizations[languageCode] ?? first entry`, else throws `MissingLocalizationException`.

**`JournalQuestionSet`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_question_set.dart`
```dart
required String id;
required Translations name;
Translations? description;
bool? isPremium;
@Default(<JournalQuestion>[]) List<JournalQuestion> questions;  // hydrated, ordered
```

**`JournalQuestionSetDto`** — `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/dtos/journal_question_set_dto.dart` — this is the **Firestore wire shape**. Same fields but `List<String> questionIds` instead of embedded questions. `toJournalQuestionSet()` joins ids against a question map; **missing ids are silently dropped** (logged as a warning, set still returned shorter than declared). Ordering is the order of `questionIds`.

### Where sets live: Firestore, not assets

Four collections, all read at runtime (`firestore.rules`):
- `question-sets/{setId}` — public sets, world-readable to any authed user
- `journal-questions/{questionId}` — public questions
- `users/{uid}/question-sets/{setId}` — private sets
- `users/{uid}/journal-questions/{questionId}` — private questions

Providers: `public_question_sets_provider.dart:61`, `public_questions_provider.dart:14`, `private_question_sets_service.dart:47`, `private_questions_service.dart:42`. Selection resolves private-first, then public (`selected_question_set_provider.dart:59-69`), defaulting to `KT9cr1mEoilCTNC6o3mK`.

One set is **hardcoded**: `legacyQuestionSet` in `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/legacy.dart` — 10 questions, same id `KT9cr1mEoilCTNC6o3mK`, used as the `@Default` for `JournalEntry.questionSet` so pre-question-set entries still render. It's the only place you can see a full concrete set without a live Firestore.

### Could users author their own sets? **No — the machinery exists but is unreachable.**

`PrivateQuestionSetsService.putQuestionSet` / `deleteQuestionSet` / `getNewQuestionSetId` and the `PrivateQuestionsService` equivalents are fully implemented, and Firestore rules allow the writes. But grepping for callers across `app/lib`, `feature/`, and `widgetbook/` returns **nothing** outside the service files themselves. `question_sets_view.dart` has no create/edit/delete affordance — `QuestionSetsController` only exposes `setSelectedQuestionSet`, `handleCheckout`, `refresh`. So in shipped behavior: pick from predefined sets only. Private sets were a half-built feature (backend + service layer done, UI never landed).

Also worth flagging for contract v1: `question_sets_controller.dart:33-52` has premium filtering commented out with `// SUBSCRIPTION SALES DISCONTINUED. Code for demo purposes only`.

## 2. How a set got into the model context

The chosen set is **denormalized onto the journal entry**, then rendered to text at session start. Two steps:

**Step 1 — freeze the set onto the entry.** `journaling_setup_controller.dart:118-138`: on pressing the journaling-assistant button, `_updateEntryWithSelectedQuestionSet()` does `journalEntry.copyWith(questionSet: questionSet)` and writes it. The entry stores the **entire hydrated set including full question objects**, not a reference — so past entries survive set edits.

**Step 2 — render to a system message.** `journaling_assistant_controller.dart:110-123`: on build, if the chat collection is empty, send an initialization prompt.

`_createQuestionsString` (`:307-319`) is the composition point:
```dart
return '${question.id}: $questionText - $typeInstructions\n\n';
```
joined with `'\n'`. The `typeInstructions` come from `JournalingAssistantJournalQuestionAnswerTypeExtension.toLocalizedInstructions` (`/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/ui/pages/journaling_assistant/extensions/journaling_assistant_journal_question_answer_type_extension.dart`) — a pure switch on the enum to a localized string. **These are per-type constants, not per-question.** `minAnswers` never reaches the prompt.

The wrapper is a localization template, `journalingAssistantInitialPrompt` (`app_localizations_en.dart:966-974`), 5 positional args:
```
Journaling history:
{history}

The user's name is {name}. Please talk to them in english.

This conversation is about the journal entry for {entryDate}.

Now is {nowIso8601}.

Collect the following information:
{questionsString}
```
History is built by `_createJournalingHistoryString` (`:282-299`) as `{date}:\n{questionId}: {localizedQuestion} - {answersJoined}`.

Sent via `JournalingAssistantServiceImpl.sendMessage(prompt, isSystemMessage: true)`, which **prefixes the literal string `'System prompt: '`** and sets `isSystemMessage: true` on the doc (`journaling_assistant_service.dart:76-82`). The Firebase GenAI chatbot extension picks it up from `users/{userID}/journalEntries/{date}/chat`, prepends the static `CONTEXT` env var, and writes back `response`.

So the env prompt's "Each topic comes with instructions on the format and number of answers required" refers to exactly these five localized strings.

Live example of the fully rendered prompt: `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/backend/extensions/firestore-genai-chatbot/tests/conversations/opening/pete_english.txt`. **Caveat: that fixture is stale** — it says `1-5 colors` / `Multiple text-based answers`, while the current localization says `One or multiple`. Trust the localization file.

## 3. The five input types

Enum `JournalQuestionAnswerType` (`journal_question.dart:10-21`). The user's recollection maps correctly but the names differ: "multi-answer" is `text`, "long text" is `longtext`.

| Enum | JSON (`type`) | Union tag (`answerType`) | Class | Answer field & type | Multi? | Validation | Prompt instruction (EN) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `text` | `"text"` | `"text"` | `JournalContentText` | `answers: List<String>` | Yes | `length >= max(1, minAnswers)` | `One or multiple texts as a list of Strings, e.g. ["Today I learned about LLMs", ...]` |
| `longtext` | `"longtext"` | `"longtext"` | `JournalContentLongtext` | `answer: String?` | **No** | non-empty; **no length cap** | `A SINGLE text as a String, e.g. "I feel happy because..."` |
| `rating` | `"rating"` | `"rating"` | `JournalContentRating` | `rating: int?` | **No** | non-null, `!= 0`; **1–10** | `A SINGLE rating from 1 to 10 (inclusive) as an Integer, e.g. 5` |
| `emoji` | `"emoji"` | `"emoji"` | `JournalContentEmoji` | `emojis: List<String>` | Yes | `length >= max(1, minAnswers)` | `One or multiple emojis as a list of Strings, e.g. ["😊", "🌟"]` |
| `color` | `"color"` | `"color"` | `JournalContentColor` | `colors: List<String>` | Yes | `length >= max(1, minAnswers)` | `One or multiple colors in hex code format as a list of Strings, e.g. ["#FF0000", "#00FF00"]` |

All in `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/app/lib/common/models/journal_content.dart` (a freezed union, `@Freezed(unionKey: 'answerType')`). Each variant carries an `@Assert` that the embedded `question.type` matches its variant.

Per-type detail:

- **rating** — plain `int`, not double. Scale 1–10 inclusive. content.text: Now the glossary updates — this is the domain-modeling output of the grilling:

input.old_string:
## Session

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user
through up to ten **topics** and ends by producing a **journal entry**. A session
is the unit the cost ceiling is measured against (~30 sessions/month for a daily
poweruser).

## Topic

One thing the assistant asks about within a session. A topic is asked via
`ask_topic` and answered via `record_answer` — the pair is what makes a topic
distinct from a free-form chat turn.

## Input type

How a topic is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders:
`text`, `color_picker`, `mood_slider`, `multi_select`. This is the surface of the
generative UI — the model chooses the input type, the client renders it.
input.new_string:
## Session

One complete run of the Journaling Assistant: the assistant walks the user
through the **questions** of a chosen **question set** and ends by producing a
**journal entry**. A session is the unit the cost ceiling is measured against
(~30 sessions/month for a daily poweruser).

## Question

One thing the assistant asks about within a session — a concrete question text
(e.g. "What are you grateful for today?"), not an abstract theme. Asked via
`ask_question`, answered via `record_answer` — the pair is what makes a question
distinct from a free-form chat turn. One `record_answer` per question carries
the complete answer; a repeated call for the same question overwrites.
("Topic" is not a term in this project; the legacy app used it only in prompts.)

## Question set

An ordered list of questions the user picks before a session starts; the session
walks exactly that set. Sets are predefined for now; user-created sets are an
intended future capability (the legacy app built the storage for this but never
shipped the UI).

## Answer type

How a question is answered, and therefore which native widget the client renders
and what shape the answer value has: `text_list` (several short texts),
`longtext` (one text), `rating` (one integer, 1–10), `emoji` (several emojis),
`color` (several hex colors). This is the surface of the generative UI — the
answer type comes from the question, the client renders the matching widget.
For list-shaped types, multiplicity lives inside the value, never in repeated
calls; `minAnswers` on a question is the only cardinality constraint.

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.

When exploring the codebase, read `CONTEXT.md` (if it exists) so test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

## What a good test is

Tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely; tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification — "user can checkout with valid cart" tells you exactly what capability exists — and survives refactors because it doesn't care about internal structure.

See [tests.md](tests.md) for examples and [mocking.md](mocking.md) for mocking guidelines.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

When the shape of that interface is itself in question — how deep the module is, where the seam belongs, what the interface should expose — use the `/codebase-design` skill for the vocabulary. It is the shared source of the module, interface, depth, seam, adapter, leverage and locality terms, and it is a reference to consult, not a session to run.

## Anti-patterns

- **Implementation-coupled** — mocks internal collaborators, tests private methods, or verifies through a side channel (querying the database instead of using the interface). The tell: the test breaks when you refactor but behavior hasn't changed.
- **Tautological** — the assertion recomputes the expected value the way the code does (`expect(add(a, b)).toBe(a + b)`, a snapshot derived by hand the same way, a constant asserted equal to itself), so it passes by construction and can never disagree with the code. Expected values must come from an independent source of truth — a known-good literal, a worked example, the spec.
- **Horizontal slicing** — writing all tests first, then all implementation. Bulk tests verify _imagined_ behavior: you test the _shape_ of things rather than user-facing behavior, the tests go insensitive to real changes, and you commit to test structure before understanding the implementation. Work in **vertical slices** instead — one test → one implementation → repeat, each test a **tracer bullet** that responds to what the last cycle taught you.

## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.

## Code sketches (all behavior probe-verified against `ai@7.0.70`)

**(a) Client-side tool — caller supplies the result.** I ran this; I did not infer it. With no `execute`, the loop halts at `finishReason: "tool-calls"` and exposes `toolCalls`. No error is thrown.

```ts
import { generateText, tool, isStepCount, type ModelMessage } from 'ai';
import { z } from 'zod';

const askQuestion = tool({
  description: 'Ask the user a question',
  inputSchema: z.object({ question: z.string() }),
  // no execute => client-side; loop stops and hands you the call
});

const messages: ModelMessage[] = [{ role: 'user', content: 'hi' }];

while (true) {
  const r = await generateText({
    model: 'zai/glm-4.7-flash',
    tools: { askQuestion },
    stopWhen: isStepCount(10),
    messages,
  });
  messages.push(...r.response.messages);
  if (r.finishReason !== 'tool-calls') { console.log(r.text); break; }

  for (const tc of r.toolCalls) {
    const answer = await promptUser(tc.input.question); // your CLI
    messages.push({
      role: 'tool',
      content: [{
        type: 'tool-result',
        toolCallId: tc.toolCallId,
        toolName: tc.toolName,
        output: { type: 'json', value: { answer } }, // discriminated union!
      }],
    });
  }
}
```

`output` **must** be `{type:'json'|'text', value}`. Passing a raw object (the v5 style) throws `InvalidPromptError` — I verified this failure mode explicitly.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/tools-and-tool-calling

**(b) Mock-model test.** Class is `MockLanguageModelV4` from `ai/test`:

```ts
import { generateText, tool, isStepCount } from 'ai';
import { MockLanguageModelV4 } from 'ai/test';

const model = new MockLanguageModelV4({
  doGenerate: async () => ({
    content: [{ type: 'tool-call', toolCallId: 'c1', toolName: 'askQuestion',
                input: JSON.stringify({ question: 'How are you?' }) }],
    finishReason: { unified: 'tool-calls', raw: undefined }, // object, not string
    usage: { inputTokens: { total: 1, noCache: 1 },
             outputTokens: { total: 1, text: 1 } },          // nested, not flat
    warnings: [],
  }),
});
```

Two v5→v7 breaks: `finishReason` is now an object `{unified, raw}` on the *mock return*, and `usage` uses nested `{total, noCache}` / `{total, text}` objects. On the *result* object, `r.finishReason` reads back as the plain string `'tool-calls'`.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/docs/ai-sdk-core/testing

**(c) Gateway wiring.** Gateway is the default provider — a bare `'creator/model'` string just works:

```ts
// .env.local: AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=...
const r = await generateText({ model: 'zai/glm-4.7-flash', prompt: 'hi' });
```

Local (not on Vercel): set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` from an API key in the Vercel dashboard. The OIDC path (`vercel env pull`) also works but tokens expire after 12h and need `vercel dev` to auto-refresh — **use the API key for a CLI**, OIDC is the wrong tool here.
Docs: https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/ai-sdk-providers/ai-gateway

- `.nvmrc` = **24.18.0**; root `package.json` engines `>=24`, packageManager `pnpm@11.17.0`, TS **7.0.2**.
- **Skip `tsx`.** Node 24 runs `.ts` natively with no flag — I confirmed `node script.ts` works even on the v22 currently active in the shell. One constraint: `enum` and other non-erasable syntax throw `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`; use `as const` unions. Type-only imports work fine.

## Contradictions and recent changes to flag

1. **`stepCountIs` is now an alias.** The canonical v7 name is `isStepCount`; the shipped types literally export `isStepCount as stepCountIs`. Both work — prefer `isStepCount`. `maxSteps` is gone entirely.
2. **Vercel's gateway docs say "AI SDK v5 and v6"** while npm ships v7 stable. The docs lag; v7 works against the gateway (`gateway`/`createGateway` verified as live exports). Gateway base URL is `https://ai-gateway.vercel.sh/v4/ai`.
3. **The tools doc conflates approvals with results.** It shows `tool-approval-response` when asked about client-side tool results. These are distinct: `ToolContent = Array<ToolResultPart | ToolApprovalResponse>`. For a CLI answering `ask_question` you want `tool-result`, not the approval flow. My probe confirms `tool-result` is what resumes the loop.
4. **`ai` v7 also ships a `ToolLoopAgent` / `Agent` class** (exported, `Experimental_Agent` alias) if you'd rather not hand-roll the while-loop. Worth a look, but the manual loop above is what gives the CLI driver control over `ask_question`, so I'd stay with it.

Based on the search results, here's what you can do to create Vercel AI Gateway API keys:

## Creating API Keys

You can create a key from the dashboard, the Vercel CLI, or the Vercel API.

### Dashboard Method
Go to the AI Gateway API Keys page and click Create key, then name and create the key. Copy the key value immediately (you cannot retrieve it again) and save it as AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY.

### CLI Method
The CLI command format is: `vercel ai-gateway api-keys create --name <NAME> --budget <DOLLARS> --refresh-period <PERIOD>`

You can also create keys with budgets and optional refresh periods (daily, weekly, monthly, or none) using this command.

### REST API Method
You can create, view, and delete AI Gateway API keys from the dashboard, CLI, or API. The Vercel REST API documentation indicates this is supported, and Vercel Access Tokens are required to authenticate and use the Vercel API, and should be included in the Authorization header.

### Key Features
API keys work anywhere, whether it's local development, external servers, or CI pipelines, and they never expire unless you revoke them. Keys created programmatically will also appear in your team AI Gateway API Keys view, so you can see all keys in one place.

I'll leave **both** PRs unmerged: [#14](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/14) (agent skeleton, CI green, live acceptance passed) and [#15](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/15) (Entire config) are ready for your review; merge whenever you're happy.

Now your two questions:

**Public-repo security.** Your posture is already decent: protected `main` with required CI, `.env.*` gitignored, Entire redacts secrets before storing, and the API key has a $5/month budget cap. What I'd add — all repo settings, so your call (I can flip them via `gh api` if you want):

1. **Secret scanning + push protection** (Settings → Code security) — free on public repos; push protection rejects a push containing a credential before it lands. The single most valuable one.
2. **Dependabot alerts + security updates** — free, low noise at this dependency count.
3. **Actions hardening** — set default workflow permissions to read-only, and require approval for workflow runs from outside collaborators. Matters most the day a repo secret exists; right now there are none, and I'd keep it that way (evals in #3 will need the gateway key in CI — use an environment-scoped secret then, not a repo-wide one).

**Where to store the API key for cloud sessions + worktrees.** The current `.env.local` is per-checkout, so worktrees and cloud sessions won't see it. The clean setup, since this deploys to Vercel anyway:

- Make the **Vercel project env** the source of truth: `vercel link` (creates/links the project — your account, so I left it untouched) then `vercel env add AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. Any checkout or worktree then hydrates itself with `vercel env pull apps/agent/.env.local` — no key ever passes through a chat context or the repo.
- **Cloud agent sessions** don't pull from Vercel automatically: set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` once in the cloud environment's settings (claude.ai/code → environment → environment variables). The CLI already prefers `process.env`, so it Just Works there with no code change.

---

❓ **Q1** - **What does the gate actually assert?**: Three layers with very different reliability: (a) **protocol correctness** — every question asked, answers recorded with correct types, `complete_session` called (deterministic, machine-checkable); (b) **conversational behavior** — the legacy fixtures' territory: off-topic redirect, refusing to answer user questions, treating lookalikes as data (needs an LLM judge / rubric — inherently fuzzy); (c) **summary quality** (fuzziest). Which layers turn CI red, and which only report?

➡️ (a) hard-gates. (b) gates via pass-rate threshold, not per-fixture (one rubric flake shouldn't block a merge). (c) report-only until #4's benchmark gives us a baseline to gate against.

❓ **Q2** - **Simulated user: scripted or LLM?**: The legacy fixtures are scripted conversations (canned user turns). An LLM-simulated user covers more surface but adds cost + a second source of non-determinism to the CI gate.

➡️ Scripted, like the legacy fixtures. The PostHog online experiment (#5) is where real-user variability gets covered; the CI gate should be as deterministic as a real model allows.

❓ **Q3** - **Flakiness policy + when CI runs evals**: A real model in CI will flake. Options: single run per fixture (cheapest, flakiest), N runs with ≥threshold pass rate (e.g. 2-of-3), or nightly-only with a manual PR trigger. And: run on every agent-path PR (the path filter already scopes it) or less often?

➡️ Every agent-path PR, N=3 per judged fixture with 2-of-3 to pass, single run for the deterministic protocol layer. At GLM-Flash prices a full CI eval run costs well under a cent — flake resistance is cheaper than a human re-run.

❓ **Q4** - **CI needs the gateway key**: I'd create a **second** API key (`emotely-ci`, own $5/month budget so a CI retry storm can't eat the dev budget) and store it as a GitHub Actions **environment secret** (forks can't reach it; outside-collaborator runs already need your approval). Same blind CLI flow as before. OK?

➡️ Yes as described.

❓ **Q5** - **Cost: report or gate?**: The issue says "report cost per session". Gate too? A hard ceiling (e.g. fail if a session exceeds 1¢ with the model under test) catches prompt bloat and retry loops the moment they land, at the risk of failing on provider price moves.

➡️ Report always + one loose hard ceiling (an order of magnitude above expected, so it only catches pathology, not price drift). Tighten in #4 with benchmark data.

❓ **Q6** - **Fold #16 (versioned prompt) into this PR?**: Evals want to pin fixtures against a prompt version, and #16 exists because of that. Do it here — `apps/agent/prompts/session.v1.md` loaded by `runSession`, version id in the eval report?

Vercel's docs point outward to third parties (Braintrust has the Marketplace integration). There is no `@vercel/evals`.

## (b) Recommendation: raw `node --test` harness, with `autoevals` only if you want a pre-built judge

Reasoning for **this** repo:

- **Your loop is already the eval harness.** `runSession({questionSet, client, model})` takes an injectable `SessionClient`. `session.test.ts` already scripts a client with canned answers. An offline eval is that same file with a real gateway model instead of `MockLanguageModelV4`. Every framework here would wrap the exact function you can call directly — that wrapper is the only thing they add.
- **promptfoo's abstraction fights your shape.** Its simulated-user provider assumes the target speaks OpenAI chat format (`{role, content}[]`) and terminates on `###STOP###` in a text response. Your session terminates on a `complete_session` **tool call**, and your "user" answers structured widget values (a rating `7`, a `text_list`), not prose. You'd stringify tool state into pseudo-chat to satisfy promptfoo, then assert on it — losing the typed `answers` record that is the actual thing worth asserting. Its own docs note `_conversation` forces concurrency 1.
- **Evalite is a dormant dependency.** Last commit 2025-11-10, stable release Feb 2026, v1 never left beta after 16 betas. Adopting it means adopting **vitest** (displacing `node --test`) plus better-sqlite3/fastify — a stack migration to gain a UI, betting on a stalled project. Fails the boring-tooling bar on the axis that matters: maintenance.
- **CI gating is already solved.** `node --test` exit codes are your gate. promptfoo needs a *second* runner in CI (`npx promptfoo eval --fail-on-error`, separate cache, separate report), which is real ongoing surface for a solo founder.
- **PostHog covers the other half.** Since online experiments handle in-the-wild quality, the offline gate only needs to catch behavioral regressions on a handful of fixtures. That's assertions, not an eval platform.

Minimal harness (~150 lines, one new file):

- **Fixture format** — plain TS objects, not YAML: `{ name, questionSet, answers: Record<qid, JSONValue>, expect }`. Typed, refactorable, no nunjucks.
- **Simulated user** — canned answers keyed by `question_id`, i.e. your existing `SessionClient`. Skip the LLM-simulated user; it doubles cost and adds a second nondeterminism source. Add it only when you need adversarial/free-text probing (the `out-of-context-user-prompts` case).
- **Judge** — one `generateText` call with a rubric returning `{pass, reason}` via a zod schema. That's the whole of `llm-rubric`. Use a strong model as judge even while evaluating cheap candidates. `autoevals` is a reasonable drop-in here, but note it hard-depends on the `openai` package.
- **Cost** — see gotcha below.
- **Stability** — run each fixture N times, assert pass-rate ≥ threshold rather than every run green, or you'll get a flaky gate on `temperature: 1` behavior.
- **Reporting** — `node --test` gives TAP; append a cost/pass-rate summary line per model.

## (c) Legacy fixture shape

Located at `/Users/petertrost/dev/emotely-legacy/backend/extensions/firestore-genai-chatbot/tests/`.

- **Encoding**: `promptfooconfig.yaml` points at a single nunjucks-templated `conversation-template.json` that renders a Gemini-format `[{role, parts:[{text}]}]` array. Each test supplies `vars.openerPrompt` (a `file://` .txt) plus an optional `messages` list of `role: text` pairs (`model:`/`user:`/`system:`). Context is injected by `getContext.js`; provider is `google:gemini-1.5-flash` at `temperature: 1`, judge is `openai:gpt-4o-mini`.
- **Assertions**: overwhelmingly `llm-rubric` (natural-language rubrics), plus a few `contains` / `not-icontains`. No `javascript` assertions. Examples: "ensure that the output does not indicate that the conversation is ending", "ensure that the output contains only a single question".
- **Four scenarios**: `opening/` (greets by name, single question, no date/time, JSON `summary: null`), `question-lookalikes/` (user answer that reads like a question), `user-ends-conversation-lookalikes/` ("No, that's all for today" must not end the session), `out-of-context-user-prompts/` (deflect a weather question back to journaling).
- **Porting reality — the fixtures do not survive intact in any tool.** As you suspected, this config targets one prompt+context producing **one text completion**, with the conversation hand-written as a fixed transcript. Our agent instead emits *tool calls*, and the transcript is generated by the loop. What ports is the **intent** of each rubric, not the YAML. Roughly equal work into promptfoo or raw TS (rewrite ~10 rubrics as judge prompts + restructure conversations as canned answer maps); promptfoo additionally makes you keep nunjucks and the pseudo-chat encoding. Note several rubrics are now **obsolete by construction** — "output contains a JSON object with `summary` null" is enforced by the `complete_session` zod schema, and "asks only one question" by the `ask_question` tool contract. Those become type assertions, not LLM judgments, which is a strict improvement.

## (d) Gotchas

- **Gateway cost is NOT in the response metadata.** I checked the installed types (`@ai-sdk/gateway@4.0.56`, `dist/index.d.ts`): `providerMetadata.gateway` carries **`generationId`**, and there is **no `cost` field** on it. (A web search claimed `gateway.cost` exists — that is wrong; I verified against the shipped `.d.ts`.) To get money you call `gateway.getGenerationInfo({ id })`, which returns `totalCost`, `upstreamInferenceCost`, `promptTokens`, `completionTokens`, `latency`, etc. **Implications**: one extra API round-trip *per generation*, and your session makes one `generateText` call per round — so a 2-question session is ~5 lookups. Cheaper alternative: sum `result.usage` tokens across rounds (free, already in the response) and multiply by the model's published rate; use `getGenerationInfo` only for spot-checking. There's also `getCredits()` for balance and a spend-report API for aggregates. Note generation lookups may lag slightly behind the request.
- **Custom Reporting is a paid add-on** ($0.075/1k tag writes, **$5 per 1,000 queries** to the reporting endpoint) — don't wire per-generation reporting queries into a CI gate that runs on every PR.
- **promptfoo cost is manual with a custom provider.** `ProviderResponse.cost` exists, but nothing computes it for you when the provider is your own function — you'd do the same token math anyway, so promptfoo buys you no cost tracking here. Its `stats` include `tokenUsage` but the summary shape has no cost field.
- **promptfoo means a second CI runner** (`npx promptfoo eval --fail-on-error`, separate `~/.cache/promptfoo` cache key, separate report artifact) living alongside `node --test`.
- **Evalite requires adopting vitest** and pulls better-sqlite3 (native build) + fastify. Its cost reporting is absent, and v1 is beta-only.
- **autoevals pulls the `openai` package** as a hard dependency even if you judge through the gateway.
- **Non-determinism**: the legacy config ran at `temperature: 1`. Set `temperature: 0` for candidate models where supported, and still gate on an N-run pass-rate threshold — a single-run all-green assertion on LLM behavior will flake in CI.
- **Free-tier rate limits (429)** on the gateway can flake CI if evals fan out across several candidate models in parallel; serialize or retry.
- **Judge cost is real**: an `llm-rubric` port means one judge call *per rubric per fixture per run*. With N-run stability multipliers this can exceed the cost of the sessions you're measuring — budget it, and consider judging once per session against several rubrics in a single structured call.

**Bottom line**: skip the framework. Add `apps/agent/src/session.eval.ts` (or a `*.eval.ts` glob excluded from the default `node --test` run so it doesn't hit the network on every unit-test invocation), driven by the `SessionClient` seam you already built. Reach for promptfoo only if you later need its red-team/adversarial strategies — that's the one capability none of this replicates.</result>

content.text: The model treats the goodbye-lookalike as a stop request despite the instruction — GLM-flash needs the example-driven style the legacy prompt used. Adding a worked example:

input.old_string: An answer that merely sounds final (e.g. "No, that's all for today.", "That's it.") is an answer to the CURRENT question — record it and continue with the remaining questions. input.new_string: An answer that merely sounds final is an answer to the CURRENT question, never a request to stop. Example: you ask "What did you learn today?" and the user answers "No, that's all for today." — that is their answer to this question; record it and ask the next question. Only skip remaining questions and call complete_session early when the user explicitly asks to stop the whole session (e.g. "please stop the session", "I don't want to journal anymore"). When in doubt, continue with the next question.

All 11 review threads are addressed, replied to, and resolved, and CI is green on the fix commit (`0c8b6d4`) — including the live protocol eval in the agent job. [PR #18](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/18) is ready for re-review.

The substantive changes, beyond the mechanical fixes:

- **"fail load" (CI eval step):** now fails loudly when the key is missing — only fork PRs (which can't have secrets) skip, with an explicit `::error::` otherwise.
- **Action pinning:** every `uses:` in both workflows is pinned to a commit SHA with a version comment; created [issue #19](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/issues/19) for Dependabot auto-updates of the pins (github-actions + npm ecosystems), since no existing issue covered it.
- **Judge model:** benched your suggestions live against the gateway. `deepseek-v4-flash` (both variants) and `gpt-oss-120b` **cannot hold the structured verdict schema** through the gateway (0–1 of 5 attempts); `qwen3.7-flash` holds schema but misjudges (1/5 correct); **`alibaba/qwen3.7-plus` scored 5/5 on both** and is now the default — open source, $0.40/M, and a different family than the GLM candidate it grades. No GLM-5.x exists on the gateway as of today; `glm-4.7` is still the newest zai line.
- **Prompt versioning:** `session/2026-08-21` → sequential `session/v1`, so multiple same-day changes just bump the counter.
- **Lint warnings:** all 6 non-null assertions fixed, and `noNonNullAssertion` is now an *error* — the answer to "why doesn't CI fail?" is that biome warnings don't fail `biome ci`; now this one will.
- Behavior eval also became crash-tolerant: a run where the model emits malformed tool input counts as a failed run instead of aborting the whole scenario (a real flake I hit while re-benching).

All suites re-verified after the changes: 20 unit tests, protocol eval ($0.00396 live), and all four behavior scenarios pass with the new judge.

Any rule that improves code quality, reduces errors, makes it more maintainable, or easier to review should be enabled and fail CI. This is also true for the dart analyzer later.

content.text:
Merged and synced. Now the strict-lint discussion — grounded in what's actually available:

**The good news: Biome 2.5.5 supports exactly your philosophy natively.** `"preset": "all"` turns on *every* rule across all groups (`a11y`, `complexity`, `correctness`, `nursery`, `performance`, `security`, `style`, `suspicious`) — deny-by-default, and anything we disable becomes an explicit, reviewable opt-out. That inverts the current posture (recommended + cherry-picked additions) into the smallest solution space with visible escape hatches.

My proposed shape:

- **Biome:** `preset: "all"`, then one triage pass over the existing code: every firing diagnostic is either a real fix (fix it) or a rule that genuinely fights our idiom (explicit `"off"`). Crucially, **switch `biome.json` → `biome.jsonc`** so every opt-out carries a one-line justification comment — the config becomes the documented exception list. No warnings tier at all: everything is error or documented-off.
- **TypeScript:** same philosophy at the compiler: the base config already has `strict` + `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`; add the remaining strictness flags (`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noImplicitOverride`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` — the last also keeps Node's type-stripping honest, which the earlier research flagged).
- **Dart (lands with issue #6, but decide the policy now):** `very_good_analysis` as the base — the strictest widely-maintained ruleset, and from VGV whose community is literally the README's target audience — plus the analyzer's `strict-casts`/`strict-inference`/`strict-raw-types` language modes, and `flutter analyze --fatal-infos` in CI so info-level hints fail the gate too. Same opt-out-with-comment convention in `analysis_options.yaml`.
- **Policy line in CLAUDE.md** so every future agent session inherits it: lints are deny-by-default; disabling a rule requires an in-config justification comment. (I'd skip an ADR — this is reversible and the config documents itself.)

Two genuine decisions before I build it:

1. **Nursery rules** (Biome's unstable group — rules still being stabilized): `preset: "all"` includes them, and they can churn on Biome upgrades — new rules appearing = new CI failures on an unrelated day. Max-strictness says include and absorb the churn (repo is small, upgrades are deliberate since versions are pinned); the boring-tooling instinct says exclude the group and cherry-pick like we already did with `noFloatingPromises`. I lean **include** — churn arrives only when *we* bump the pinned version, so it lands inside a PR we control.
2. **Timing:** do it now as its own PR? The codebase is ~15 files — the triage pass will never be cheaper than today, and every rule adopted before the Flutter app exists is one that never needs a migration. I'd do it now.

If you're good with both (or override either), I'll run the triage and put the PR up.
agreed on everything. We do it now.

content.text:
All green — both jobs, including the live protocol eval and the newly-strict Flutter analyze. [PR #20](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/pull/20) is up and ready for your review.

What the policy landed as:

- **Biome `preset: "all"`** in `biome.jsonc` — ~160 diagnostics triaged: the real ones fixed (explicit `node:process` imports, block statements, two complexity refactors that genuinely improved the code — `buildSessionTools` and `runScenarioOnce` extracted, named constants for cost/round math), and 13 rules disabled *with inline justifications* (wire-format snake_case, Node-service rules, sequential conversation loops, secret-scanner false positives on Firestore ids, taste rules, and two genuine conflicts: `useLiteralKeys` vs the TS index-signature flag, `noUnresolvedImports` vs pre-build lint in CI).
- **TS:** four new strictness flags; `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` documented-off because `ai@7`'s own types aren't clean under it — retry noted for the next major.
- **Dart:** `very_good_analysis` 10.3.0 + `strict-casts`/`strict-inference`/`strict-raw-types`, CI at `flutter analyze --fatal-infos`. The tutorial counter-app scaffold shrank to a minimal documented placeholder rather than getting docstring decoration (#6 replaces it anyway).
- **CLAUDE.md** carries the policy, including the rule that matters most for future agent sessions: *never fix a diagnostic by weakening a rule without an in-config justification comment.*

Tests/evals all green throughout. Merge when you've had your look — after that, the board shows [#4](https://github.com/trost-systems/emotely/issues/4) (model benchmark + gateway decision, which the eval harness now makes cheap to run) as the natural next step.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline — challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `CONTEXT.md` for vocabulary is not this skill — that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── CONTEXT.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── CONTEXT-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── CONTEXT.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── CONTEXT.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily — only when you have something to write. If no `CONTEXT.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `CONTEXT.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y — which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account' — do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"

### Update CONTEXT.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `CONTEXT.md` right there. Don't batch these up — capture them as they happen. Use the format in [CONTEXT-FORMAT.md](./CONTEXT-FORMAT.md).

`CONTEXT.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `CONTEXT.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse** — the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context** — a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off** — there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

| **Model switching** | Bare `'creator/model'` string | Bare `'creator/model'` string |
| **Routing** | `order`/`only`/`sort: 'cost'\|'ttft'\|'tps'`, provider timeouts, model fallbacks | Comparable |
| **Add-on costs** | Custom Reporting $0.075/1k writes, ZDR/allowlist $0.10/1k — **all off by default** | — |

**The ADR's deciding criterion is now void.** ADR 0003 defers the choice on "OpenRouter has a *dedicated* PostHog install path; Vercel AI Gateway is listed as 'supported'." That distinction does not survive contact with ai@7:

- PostHog's OpenRouter page installs `@posthog/ai/openai` — an **OpenAI-client wrapper**, not an AI SDK path. Adopting it means abandoning `generateText`, hand-rolling the tool loop, and **manually capturing every tool call as an `$ai_span`**. That is strictly more code than you have now.
- PostHog's Vercel AI SDK page is explicit: *"This OpenTelemetry integration is the supported path for Vercel AI SDK v7. The legacy PostHog `withTracing` wrapper supports the v5 and v6 provider interfaces and **rejects v7 models**."*
- The v7 path is a `PostHogSpanProcessor` + `registerTelemetry(new OpenTelemetry(...))` in `instrumentation.ts`. It instruments **the SDK, not the provider** — so **the gateway is invisible to PostHog**. Neither gateway has an integration advantage; the "dedicated install path" is the *worse* one here.

Net: OpenRouter costs 5.5% on credits and 5% on BYOK, and its PostHog path would force a rewrite off `generateText`. Vercel AI Gateway is 0%/0% and already works. **Decide for Vercel AI Gateway and close the deferral.**

Lock-in surface is genuinely small either way: bare model strings + an `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`. Migration = swap base URL/key. The only gateway-specific code would be `providerOptions.gateway` — which, per (d), you don't need.

## (b) Caching — automatic for every candidate, zero code

Vercel's automatic-caching doc: *"providers like OpenAI, Google, and DeepSeek cache automatically (sometimes called 'implicit caching')… For providers with implicit caching, no modification is needed and caching works automatically."* `caching: 'auto'` exists **only** to inject `cache_control` markers for Anthropic and MiniMax. Note `implicit-caching` is a per-model catalog tag, not a per-request setting — and cheap models with large static prefixes are exactly the case it pays off on. Prices $/Mtok:

## (d) Code changes for prompt caching: **none required** — but your cost math is wrong

Caching needs no code. However, `apps/agent/src/session.ts:135-136` accumulates only `inputTokens`/`outputTokens`, and `cost.ts` multiplies input by a single `inputPerM`. I confirmed from the installed `ai@7.0.70` source (`asLanguageModelUsage`) that:

```js
inputTokens: usage.inputTokens.total,
inputTokenDetails: { noCacheTokens: ..., cacheReadTokens: ..., cacheWriteTokens: ... }
```

**`inputTokens` is the total and is inclusive of cache reads.** So today the cost model bills every cached token at full rate — it will **overstate cost and hide the entire caching win**, the 3-5× the ADR is banking on. Two corrections:

- The field is **`inputTokenDetails.cacheReadTokens`**, not `usage.cachedInputTokens` or `inputTokens.cacheRead` as the task assumed — neither exists in ai@7.
- **`result.totalUsage` is `@deprecated` in ai@7.0.70; use `result.usage`.** Both lines in `session.ts` use the deprecated field.

Minimum fix: track `cacheReadTokens`, add `cacheReadPerM` to `ModelRates`, and bill `(inputTokens - cacheReadTokens)` at input rate plus `cacheReadTokens` at the cache rate. That's a few lines in `cost.ts` plus one accumulator — and it's what makes the #4 benchmark measure the thing that actually decides the model.

## (e) Contradictions with ADR 0003

1. **The deferral criterion is dead.** "OpenRouter has a *dedicated* PostHog install path" no longer favors OpenRouter — on ai@7 that path is an OpenAI-client wrapper requiring manual `$ai_span` capture, while `withTracing` *rejects v7 models*. The v7 OTel path is gateway-agnostic. Recommend closing the deferral for Vercel AI Gateway.
2. **"Both work with PostHog LLM observability" is true but for a different reason than stated** — PostHog instruments the AI SDK, not the provider, so the gateway is irrelevant to observability. Integration cleanliness cannot decide this; **fees and BYOK should** (0%/0% vs 5.5%/5%).
3. **"Prompt caching on the static context prompt"** understates it. The ~1k static system prompt is the small half; the real win is the **growing conversation prefix** across 25 rounds, which implicit caching covers automatically at 5-10× discounts.
4. **`MODEL_RATES` in `cost.ts` is already stale in shape** — no cache-read rate, so it cannot express the ADR's own 3-5× savings claim.
5. **A cheaper candidate exists now** (`qwen3.7-flash`, released after the ADR), reinforcing that the model list should be regenerated from the live catalog at benchmark time.

## Amendment 2026-08-22: gateway decided, ceiling revised

**Gateway: Vercel AI Gateway.** The deferral's deciding criterion ("OpenRouter
has a dedicated PostHog install path") did not survive the AI SDK v7 research:
PostHog's supported v7 path is an OpenTelemetry span processor that instruments
the SDK, not the provider, so observability is gateway-agnostic — and the
"dedicated" OpenRouter path is an OpenAI-client wrapper that would force us off
`generateText`. What remains is fees: Vercel AI Gateway charges 0% on tokens and
0% on BYOK; OpenRouter 5.5% on credits and 5% on BYOK. Lock-in is one env var
plus bare `creator/model` strings either way.

**Ceiling: ≤ €1/month per daily poweruser (≈ $0.036/session at 30 sessions),
and within that, the fastest reliable model wins.** Margins inside a €5
subscription are fine at that level, and GenUI latency is what the user feels
between widgets. This replaces "well under 50¢, frontier out": Haiku-class and
the small frontier tiers (e.g. GPT-5.6 Luna at $0.20/M in) are eligible
candidates, ranked by median per-round latency with cost as tiebreak. We start
reliable and fast, and optimize toward cheaper models with real usage data.

**Caching needs no code.** Every gateway candidate is implicitly cached; the
win is the growing conversation prefix across ~25 rounds, not just the static
prompt. Measured, not assumed: the first live reading for glm-4.7-flash was
`cached=0` despite its catalog tag.

Selection is re-run monthly by a scheduled benchmark that also lists new
tool-capable models from the live catalog (issue #4).
EOF
echo "ADR amended"
